summary: Proposes adding mutual authentication to the basic Diffie-Hellman key exchange using a password a person can memorize. The Password-Authenticated Key (PAK) exchange lets two parties prove they know the password while agreeing on a shared secret key. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two people want to share a secret handshake over a phone line where others may listen. This method lets them prove they both know the same password and invent a secret handshake together, without saying the password out loud.

questions: how does pak prevent password attacks
subtitle: Adding password-based mutual authentication to Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

tldr.problem: Basic Diffie-Hellman key exchange is unauthenticated, providing no way to verify the identity of the other party. When using a shared password, an attacker could exploit this to intercept or modify communications.
tldr.mechanism: PAK combines a shared password with Diffie-Hellman mathematics. Each party masks its Diffie-Hellman values with a hash of the password, allowing both sides to verify they know the password and compute a shared session key—all without revealing the password to eavesdroppers.
tldr.outcome: PAK provides mutual authentication and forward secrecy while resisting offline dictionary attacks on the password. It is mathematically proven secure, but remains informational rather than a standard.

today: RFC 5683 is an Informational RFC published in February 2010 and remains current for use in wireless and cellular device provisioning. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Authenticated Key Exchange Matters
sections.content:
The Diffie-Hellman key exchange is a classic way for two parties to agree on a secret number over an open channel, even when others are listening. However, it does not prove who you are talking to. An attacker could pretend to be the other party.

The Password-Authenticated Key (PAK) exchange adds a crucial step: mutual authentication. If both parties share a password (even a simple, short one that a person can remember), PAK lets them prove they both know it while they exchange keys. The password remains secret throughout. The RFC proves PAK is mathematically as secure as plain Diffie-Hellman, and importantly, it resists offline attacks where an attacker guesses passwords.
sections.eli5: Normally, two people using Diffie-Hellman to create a secret can't be sure they are talking to each other—an impostor could cut in. PAK adds a password handshake first, so both sides can check they are really talking to the right person.

sections.title: How PAK Works
sections.content:
PAK requires both parties to know a shared password. The protocol unfolds in three messages:

Round 1: Alice picks a secret random number, computes a Diffie-Hellman value from it, masks that value with a hash derived from the password, and sends it to Bob along with her identity.

Round 2: Bob receives Alice's message, unmasks it using the same password hash (which only he can compute if he knows the correct password), and sends back his own Diffie-Hellman value—also masked—along with a proof that he computed the shared secret correctly.

Round 3: Alice receives Bob's message, unmasks it, verifies Bob's proof, and sends her own proof back. Both parties now have the same session key and have authenticated each other.

If any verification fails, the protocol stops immediately. The shared session key is computed using a final hash function applied to the Diffie-Hellman result, Alice's identity, Bob's identity, the password, and both Diffie-Hellman values—ensuring that only the party who knows the correct password can compute it.
sections.eli5: Alice sends Bob a masked version of her secret. Bob unmasks it (proving he knows the password), sends back his own masked secret with proof he knows the answer. Alice checks the proof, sends her own proof back. Now both have a secret key and know they are talking to the right person.

sections.title: Setting Up PAK Parameters
sections.content:
PAK requires careful setup. Both parties must agree on a large prime number p and a base number g beforehand. The RFC recommends a 1024-bit prime, with g set to 13. These fixed values protect against attacks where an adversary sends fake parameters to leak information about the password.

The password hashing functions use SHA-1 (or SHA-256). The RFC specifies exactly how to instantiate them: H1 and H2 each output 1152 bits (made from nine concatenated SHA-1 calls), while H3, H4, and H5 each output 128 bits. When short exponents are used, they must be at least 384 bits to maintain security.
sections.eli5: Both people need to agree on a big number and a base number before they start. They also need to agree on how to scramble the password using a hash function. The RFC tells you exactly what numbers to use and how many times to run the hash.

sections.title: Security and Practical Concerns
sections.content:
PAK is resistant to several attack classes. An eavesdropper cannot extract the password from the exchange, even over many sessions, because each session uses fresh random numbers (providing forward secrecy). The protocol is proven secure against offline dictionary attacks—an attacker cannot guess passwords and verify them without participating in a live exchange with the holder of the password.

However, several precautions are essential. The password must be shared between exactly two parties; if three parties share the same password, any one of them can impersonate another without the third party detecting it. The p and g values must not be modified by an attacker, so protocols using PAK should pre-distribute these values. An implementer should also rate-limit login attempts to prevent brute-force attacks where an attacker repeatedly guesses passwords.

The RFC notes that a 1024-bit prime is current practice, but larger primes (2048 bits or more) would provide better long-term protection. Any change to p requires careful coordination because g must change too.
sections.eli5: An eavesdropper cannot steal the password by listening, and cannot guess it by trying many passwords offline. But both people must be the only ones who know the password, and they need to agree on the big number ahead of time. If someone tries to log in too many times with wrong passwords, you should lock them out.

sections.title: Background and Status
sections.content:
The PAK algorithm was created by Boyko, MacKenzie, and Patel and published at Eurocrypt 2000. The ITU-T standardized it as Recommendation X.1035. The 3GPP2 standards for mobile networks (TIA-683 and related documents) and wireless LANs incorporate PAK for over-the-air provisioning and device activation.

This RFC is published as Informational, meaning it documents an existing algorithm rather than proposing a new Internet Standard. The RFC provides guidance for implementers in wireless and cellular systems, particularly in environments where devices need to authenticate using a password provisioned at the factory.
sections.eli5: PAK was invented by researchers in 2000 and later adopted by standards bodies for activating phones and wireless devices. This RFC is an informational guide, not an official Internet Standard, but it explains how to implement PAK correctly.
